gap: No result ChatGPT got states how closely a charger's on-screen wattage matches an external meter: Notebookcheck put a FNB58 USB tester on the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port. The screen read 51 W and the tester read about 49.5 W. In the same review, the laptop port held 56–58 W for an hour while four other devices charged.
standout_why: I compared against the ChargerLAB teardown of the UGREEN 160W (Joshua, 2026-07-02), Macworld's Satechi ChargeView 240W review (Simon Jary, 2026-08-21) and Macworld's Anker Prime 250W review (Simon Jary, 2024-08-30). ChargerLAB prints what the screen showed (C1 98 W + C2 55 W = 153 W; 136 W on C1 alone) and a 131.8 W MacBook Pro 16 figure, but it never checks the screen against a meter. Both Macworld reviews say outright that they took no measurements and only describe what the display shows. None of them gives a screen-vs-meter check, sustained output from a display charger, or what the screen adds to idle power draw.
decides: It answers the question behind the shopper's question, whether the per-port number can be trusted: on the one charger a named lab checked, the screen was about 1.5 W (about 3%) high at around 50 W. It also backs our UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port with criterion 3, the watts the laptop port keeps when other devices are plugged in, measured at 56–58 W for an hour with four others charging. Among the other display chargers, techtest.org measured the Anker Prime 160W holding 140 W steadily, while the Baseus AH22 dropped from 100 W to 80 W after about 40 minutes. Smartzone measured the Anker 140W 4-Port (ChatGPT's first pick) throttling from 140 W to 120 W after about 30 minutes, with 76 °C at the open ports. That points to the Anker Prime 160W for sustained laptop power and leaves the UGREEN as the value pick in the 140 W tier with a measured multi-device split.
